body.statement: For every finite \(\mathcal H_0\subset[-H,H]^K\), the fixed Gaussian grid experiment is exactly embedded by vertex controls in the score diffusion, and the strict extension from the regular-payoff results of Wager and Xu and Adusumilli holds: arbitrary predictable policies, zero-allocation faces, and the discontinuous closed-test terminal loss satisfy \(\sup_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}|B_n(\lambda)-B(\lambda)|\to0\), \(c_{n,m}\to c_m\) for every \(m\), and \(V_n\to V\). Moreover, for each \(\epsilon>0\) there are predictable finite-horizon policies whose scenario-risk vectors converge coordinatewise to that of an \(\epsilon\)-optimal diffusion control.
body.proof_tex:
We prove separately the exact embedding, regular-payoff approximation, the
boundary squeeze, and policy attainment.

\emph{Exact embedding.}
Fix \(n\) and \(\pi_n\in\Pi_n\).  On
\(((i-1)/n,i/n]\), let the continuous control be the vertex
\[
u_j(t)=\mathbf 1\{A_i=j\}.
\]
It is observed-filtration predictable by Assumption
\(\mathrm{ass:finite\text{-}predictability}\), hence admissible under
Assumption \(\mathrm{ass:continuous\text{-}observed\text{-}control}\).
Conditionally on the history and \(A_i=j\), its score increment is
\[
\Delta X_j=\frac{h_j^m}{n}
+W_j(i/n)-W_j((i-1)/n)
\sim\mathcal N(h_j^m/n,1/n),
\]
and its clock increment is \(1/n\); all other coordinates have zero
increments.  By Assumptions \(\mathrm{ass:gaussian\text{-}known\text{-}variance}\)
and \(\mathrm{ass:local\text{-}scenario\text{-}scaling}\),
\(Y_i/\sqrt n\) has exactly the same conditional law.  Induction over \(i\)
therefore gives equality of the complete observed laws, not merely weak
convergence.  Thus every finite policy is a vertex-control diffusion policy
and has exactly the same risk vector.

\emph{Approximation for continuous terminal payoffs.}
Let \(g_m:\mathbb R^K\times[0,1]^K\to[0,1]\) be bounded and continuous, for
\(m=1,\ldots,M\).  We claim that the infimal prior-weighted risk over the
embedded \(n\)-grid controls converges to the infimum over \(\mathcal U\).
Here is the construction in the present Gaussian experiment.

On the canonical observed space, every progressively measurable
\(\Delta(\mathcal J)\)-valued control is approximable in
\(dt\,d\mathbb P_0\)-measure by simple predictable controls: first replace it
by conditional averages on a deterministic time partition, and then
approximate each past-measurable simplex-valued random variable by a finite
simple function.  Boundedness upgrades convergence in measure to
\[
\mathbb E_0\int_0^1\sum_j|u_j^{(r)}(t)-u_j(t)|\,dt\longrightarrow0.
\tag{7}
\]
For a fixed simple control, subdivide each of its time cells into \(n\)-grid
cells and, conditionally on the information at the left endpoint, choose
vertex \(j\) with its declared simplex probability.  Conditional variances
of the centered allocation counts sum to at most \(1/n\), so the cumulative
clock error tends to zero in probability.  Conditional on those counts, the
score increment in coordinate \(j\) is exactly Gaussian with mean
\(h_j^m\Delta Q_j\) and variance \(\Delta Q_j\).  Therefore its conditional
characteristic function is
\[
\exp\!\left\{\mathrm i z_jh_j^m\Delta Q_j
-\frac12z_j^2\Delta Q_j\right\},
\]
which converges to the characteristic function of the corresponding relaxed
Gaussian transition.  Induction over the finitely many simple-control cells
proves joint convergence of the terminal score and clock.  Past-measurable
simple functions may be chosen continuous outside sets of arbitrarily small
probability under all of the finitely many scenario laws; changing them on
those sets changes any bounded risk by at most that probability.  A diagonal
choice in \(r\) and \(n\) therefore gives grid policies
\(\pi_n[u]\) such that
\[
(X_n,Q_n)\ \Longrightarrow\ (X^u(1),Q^u(1))
\quad\text{under every }m.
\tag{8}
\]
This construction uses vertex choices even when some simplex coordinates
are zero, so it imposes no exploration lower bound.

One can also see directly that the change from the reference law to every
scenario is harmless in (8).  Under drift zero, the likelihood ratio is
\[
Z_m(X,Q)=
\exp\!\left\{\sum_jh_j^mX_j-\frac12
\sum_j(h_j^m)^2Q_j\right\}.
\tag{9}
\]
The assignment factors cancel because the policy is scenario independent.
Furthermore,
\[
\mathbb E_0[Z_m(X,Q)^2]
\leq\exp(H^2),
\tag{10}
\]
because \(\sum_jQ_j=1\) and \(|h_j^m|\leq H\).  Thus the likelihood ratios
are uniformly integrable, and reference-law convergence transfers to all
\(M\) scenario laws.  Equations (7)--(10), bounded continuity of \(g_m\),
and an \(\varepsilon\)-optimal choice of \(u\) show
\[
\inf_{\pi_n\in\Pi_n}\sum_m\lambda_m\mathbb E_m^{\pi_n}g_m
\longrightarrow
\inf_{u\in\mathcal U}\sum_m\lambda_m\mathbb E_m^ug_m
\tag{11}
\]
for each \(\lambda\).  The reverse inequality needed in (11) holds at every
\(n\) because of the exact embedding.  This proves the regular-payoff
approximation from the primitive Gaussian transitions rather than assuming
a limit law.

For fixed \(\delta>0\), the functions
\(\ell_{m,\delta}^\pm\) from Definition
\(\mathrm{def:terminal\text{-}envelopes}\) are bounded and continuous:
exponentiation, finite averages, and finite minima are continuous, as are
\(f_\delta^\pm\).  Applying (11) yields
\[
B_{n,\delta}^\pm(\lambda)\longrightarrow
B_\delta^\pm(\lambda).
\tag{12}
\]
Every one of the four value functions in (12) is \(1\)-Lipschitz in
\(\lambda\) for the \(\ell_1\) norm, because each scenario risk lies in
\([0,1]\).  A finite \(\ell_1\)-net of the compact simplex \(\Delta_M\)
therefore upgrades (12) to convergence uniform in \(\lambda\).

\emph{Removal of the continuous envelopes.}
The scalar bracketing proved in
\(\mathrm{lem:quantitative\text{-}terminal\text{-}comparison}\) gives
\[
B_{n,\delta}^-(\lambda)\leq B_n(\lambda)\leq
B_{n,\delta}^+(\lambda),
\qquad
B_\delta^-(\lambda)\leq B(\lambda)\leq B_\delta^+(\lambda).
\]
Combining these inequalities with (12) gives
\[
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\sup_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}
|B_n(\lambda)-B(\lambda)|
\leq\rho_{H,K}(\delta,\sqrt\delta).
\]
Letting \(\delta\downarrow0\) and using the last conclusion of
\(\mathrm{lem:quantitative\text{-}terminal\text{-}comparison}\) proves
\[
\sup_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}|B_n(\lambda)-B(\lambda)|\longrightarrow0.
\tag{13}
\]
For the point-mass prior \(e_m\), the definitions give
\(B_n(e_m)=c_{n,m}\) and \(B(e_m)=c_m\).  Hence (13) proves
\[
\max_{1\leq m\leq M}|c_{n,m}-c_m|\longrightarrow0.
\tag{14}
\]

For completeness, we derive the finite-scenario minimax identity needed to
pass from (13)--(14) to regret values.  Let \(C_n\) be the closure in
\([0,1]^M\) of the achievable regret vectors.  Independent randomization at
time zero makes it convex, and closure makes it compact without changing the
infimum of any continuous criterion.  Since
\(\max_m r_m=\max_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}\lambda^\top r\), finite-dimensional
convex separation gives
\[
\inf_{r\in C_n}\max_mr_m
=\max_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}\inf_{r\in C_n}\lambda^\top r.
\tag{15}
\]
To verify the direction in (15), put \(v=\inf_{r\in C_n}\max_mr_m\).
The upward-closed convex set \(C_n+\mathbb R_+^M\) has \(v\mathbf1\) on its
boundary.  Projecting \((v-k^{-1})\mathbf1\) onto this set and taking a
convergent subsequence of the normalized projection normals produces
\(\lambda\geq0\), \(\sum_m\lambda_m=1\), with
\(\lambda^\top r\geq v\) for every \(r\in C_n\).  The opposite inequality
follows from \(\lambda^\top r\leq\max_mr_m\).  This proves (15)
elementarily.  Translating back from regret to loss yields
\[
V_n=\max_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}
\left\{B_n(\lambda)-\sum_m\lambda_mc_{n,m}\right\},
\]
and the identical argument gives the corresponding formula for \(V\).
Consequently,
\[
|V_n-V|
\leq\sup_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}|B_n(\lambda)-B(\lambda)|
+\max_m|c_{n,m}-c_m|\longrightarrow0
\]
by (13)--(14).

\emph{Predictable policy attainment.}
Fix \(\epsilon>0\).  Choose a finite integer \(N\) so large that
\(|V_N-V|+\max_m|c_{N,m}-c_m|<\epsilon/3\), and choose
\(\pi_N\in\Pi_N\) with
\[
\max_m\{L_N(\pi_N,m)-c_{N,m}\}\leq V_N+\epsilon/3.
\]
Embed \(\pi_N\) as the \(N\)-block vertex control \(u^\epsilon\) constructed
above.  Exact equality of risk vectors and the preceding bounds show
\[
\max_m r_m(u^\epsilon)\leq V+\epsilon.
\tag{16}
\]
This is an \(\epsilon\)-optimal diffusion control.

It remains to approximate this particular control without invoking
continuity of an arbitrary stopped diffusion payoff.  Conditional on an
exogenous random seed and on any of the finitely many action sequences of
\(\pi_N\), the \(N\) observed Gaussian outcomes have a Lebesgue density.
Every terminal threshold equality is contained in a finite union of zero
sets of functions
\[
\sum_{j\in I}\exp(X_j-Q_j/2)-20|I|.
\]
Such a function is nonconstant whenever one of its coordinates was sampled;
if none was sampled its value is \(|I|-20|I|\neq0\).  Its zero set therefore
has Lebesgue measure zero.  Hence
\[
\Pr_m^{u^\epsilon}\{a_j(X(1),Q(1))=0
\text{ for some }j\}=0
\quad\text{for every }m.
\tag{17}
\]
At horizon \(n\), divide the observations into \(N\) consecutive blocks
whose lengths differ from \(n/N\) by at most one, keep the arm selected by
\(\pi_N\) throughout a block, and feed the next decision the block aggregate.
This is a predictable finite policy.  Each aggregate is exactly Gaussian
with clock length converging to \(1/N\); induction over the fixed number
\(N\) of blocks gives convergence of its terminal state to that of
\(u^\epsilon\).  Arbitrary measurable recruitment kernels of \(\pi_N\) may
first be changed on sets of arbitrarily small probability under the finite
family of Gaussian history laws so that this induction is valid at their
continuity points.  Equation (17) then permits the ordinary bounded
continuous-mapping argument for the original strict miss indicators.
Thus the resulting predictable policies \(\pi_n^\epsilon\) satisfy
\[
L_n(\pi_n^\epsilon,m)\longrightarrow L(u^\epsilon,m)
\quad\text{for every }m.
\]
Together with (16), this proves the asserted coordinatewise risk transfer.
The construction permits zero block allocations to every unused subgroup,
so arbitrary predictable policies and zero-allocation faces are retained.
Assumption \(\mathrm{ass:null\text{-}boundary\text{-}closure}\) ensures that
all intersection-null boundary projections invoked by the declared design
remain within the fixed finite scenario set; the auxiliary common drift used
in the comparison proof is only a change-of-measure device and does not
enlarge that set.
body.justification: It identifies the attainable local-power regret frontier for the fixed confirmatory test.
body.gap: Adusumilli's 2026 theorem gives subsequential allocation-process representations and Adusumilli's 2025 convergence theorem uses Hölder data; this theorem adds a discontinuous closure payoff and legal boundary atoms.
body.consumer: It converts a continuum recruitment solution into asymptotically valid finite-stage policies for interAdapt-style designs.
